answer: The latest article in the BBC News Green Living section (https://www.bbc.com/future-planet/green-living) is 'The Himalayan village where you can see the cosmos', published 1 September 2025 (https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20250829-the-himalayan-village-where-you-can-see-the-cosmos). Main points: (1) Hanle, a remote village in the barren, Moon-like landscape of Ladakh in northern India, has some of the darkest skies on Earth, rating 'one' (the darkest) on the Bortle dark-sky scale with about 270 clear nights a year, so the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye. (2) Since the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve was founded in 2022 - spanning 1,074 sq km, six villages, a monastery and 10 stationary telescopes - astrotourism has flourished, with homestays and trained local astro guides running stargazing expeditions. (3) The village hosts the Indian Astronomical Observatory on Mount Digpa Ratsa Ri, home to one of the world's highest optical telescopes (the Himalayan Chandra Telescope) and MACE, the world's second-largest gamma-ray telescope. (4) Hanle's annual Star Party, held each September during the brief four-month accessible window, draws stargazers and astrophotographers from across India. (5) Rising tourism brings income but also light-pollution concerns: villagers switch off lights at dusk (no power after 23:00), use blackout curtains and warm bulbs, and the Indian Institute of Astrophysics is adding measures such as road delineators and plans to decentralise astrotourism across Ladakh. (6) Practical tips: visit June-September around the new Moon, fly Delhi to Leh and acclimatise, arrange permits in advance and book homestays early.
